stem: During an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, its internal-energy change is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Assumes the gas gains internal energy because it takes in heat while expanding, ignoring that for an ideal gas at constant temperature the heat absorbed is converted entirely to work.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Assumes the gas loses internal energy as it does work expanding, ignoring that the heat absorbed isothermally exactly offsets it.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: ideal-gas internal energy depends only on temperature

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Confuses internal energy with pressure, treating the two as numerically interchangeable rather than recognizing internal energy depends only on temperature.

stem: Which of the following best explains why energy is spontaneously transferred from a hot object to a cold object?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The transfer decreases the total entropy of the system
choices.rationale: Reverses the direction required by the second law of thermodynamics for a spontaneous process.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The transfer increases the total entropy of the system
choices.rationale: spontaneous heat transfer increases total entropy

choices.label: C
choices.text: The transfer violates conservation of energy
choices.rationale: Confuses entropy increase with a violation of energy conservation, when heat flow conserves energy while still increasing entropy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The transfer decreases the entropy of the cold object
choices.rationale: Reverses the actual effect: heat flowing into the cold object increases its entropy, and because the cold object is at the lower temperature (ΔS ≈ Q/T_c for a small transfer) that increase is larger than the hot object's decrease (≈ Q/T_h), so the total entropy increases.

stem: The electric field direction at a point is the direction of force on

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: field direction is defined using a positive test charge

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Reverses the sign convention, treating the field as defined by the force on a negative test charge.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: A neutral object has no sign of charge, so the force on it cannot define the field direction, whereas the field direction is defined by the force on a positive test charge.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Treats the definition as applying to one particular particle. The field direction is defined by the force on a positive test charge, whatever the sign of the charges that create the field; the force on an electron points opposite to the field.

stem: Moving a positive charge opposite a uniform electric field causes electric potential energy to

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Assumes moving against the field lowers potential energy, as if borrowing the sign convention from motion with a field (or gravity) rather than against it.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Moving a positive charge opposite the field requires positive work by an external force, so the electric potential energy of the charge increases.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Potential energy would stay constant only for motion perpendicular to the field (along an equipotential). Moving opposite the field requires positive work by an external force, so the potential energy changes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: become negative regardless of the starting value
choices.rationale: Assumes the change always produces a negative value. Moving against the field adds energy equal to the positive external work, so the potential energy rises from whatever it was; the sign of the final value depends on the starting value and the reference point.

stem: Two identical positive point charges are placed on a horizontal line, one to the left of the other. At the midpoint between them, the electric field is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The two charges are equal in magnitude and equidistant from the midpoint, so the electric field each produces there has equal magnitude. Because both charges are positive, each field points away from its own charge, meaning the two fields point in opposite directions at the midpoint. Equal-magnitude, opposite-direction vectors sum to zero, giving a net field of zero.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Accounts only for the right charge's field at the midpoint (which points toward the left), ignoring the left charge's opposing contribution.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Accounts only for the left charge's field at the midpoint (which points toward the right), ignoring the right charge's opposing contribution.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The midpoint is a finite distance from both charges, so each field is finite and the two fields cancel.

stem: Two resistors 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel have equivalent resistance

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: reciprocal addition gives 2 ohms

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Picks the smaller resistor value directly, as if it alone set the parallel combination without performing the reciprocal sum.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Adds the resistances as if they were in series instead of combining them in parallel.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Stops partway through the product-over-sum shortcut, taking only the product of the two resistances without dividing by their sum.

stem: A 12 V battery drives 3 A through a resistor. Its resistance is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Inverts the formula, computing I/V instead of V/I.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: R=V/I

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Subtracts the given values (12-3=9) instead of dividing voltage by current.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Multiplies the given values (12x3=36) instead of dividing voltage by current.

stem: Immediately after an uncharged capacitor is connected through a resistor to a battery, the capacitor behaves approximately like

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Describes the capacitor's long-time steady-state behavior, once it is fully charged and blocks current, rather than its initial state.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: initial capacitor voltage is zero

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Assumes the capacitor starts fully charged and able to supply voltage, the opposite of its actual initial uncharged state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a resistor with the same resistance as the series resistor
choices.rationale: Treats the capacitor as additional resistance that limits the current. At the first instant the uncharged capacitor has zero potential difference, so it adds no opposition and the current is set by the resistor alone, battery voltage divided by R.

stem: At fixed temperature and volume, doubling the number of ideal-gas molecules makes pressure

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies an inverse relation between pressure and molecule count.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This ignores the added molecular collisions with the container walls.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: From PV=NkT, pressure is directly proportional to molecule count at fixed V and T.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This incorrectly squares the factor by which molecule count changes.

stem: Two rods have equal dimensions and temperature difference. Rod A has twice Rod B's thermal conductivity. The steady conduction rate through A is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This reverses the conductivity dependence, treating better conduction as slower transfer.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This ignores the only property that differs between the rods.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Conduction rate kAΔT/L is directly proportional to thermal conductivity k.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This squares the conductivity factor even though the relation is linear.

stem: Two different ideal gases initially separated at the same temperature mix in an insulated container. The total entropy

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This reverses the second-law direction for spontaneous mixing.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This treats insulation as preventing entropy change rather than preventing energy transfer.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Spontaneous mixing increases the number of accessible arrangements and therefore total entropy.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This confuses an arbitrary entropy reference with the positive mixing change.

stem: Identical isolated conducting spheres carry charges +6Q and 0. They touch and separate. After separating, the two spheres' charges are

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This assumes no charge redistribution occurs between identical conductors in contact, but touching connects the spheres electrically, letting charge flow until both reach the same potential.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Total charge +6Q is conserved. Since the spheres are identical (same capacitance), touching brings them to equal potential, which requires equal final charge: +3Q each.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This duplicates the original charge instead of redistributing it, violating conservation of charge (total would become +12Q).

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This assumes complete neutralization, but there is no negative charge present to cancel the +6Q -- conservation of charge requires the total to remain +6Q.

stem: At a point where electric potential is zero, the electric field

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This confuses a potential reference value with zero potential change.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: Zero potential at one point says nothing about whether the field is uniform. The field is set by how quickly the potential changes with position, and that can differ from point to point near the zero-potential point.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Potential value can be zero while its spatial change, and hence electric field, is nonzero.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: Electric-field direction depends on the spatial decrease of potential, not on whether the potential value at one point is zero.

stem: An electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of magnitude ΔV gains kinetic energy equal to

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: The kinetic-energy gain magnitude is |qΔV|=eΔV, by the work-energy theorem applied to the electric force.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This incorrectly carries the 1/2 from the kinetic-energy expression (1/2)mv² into the answer; the work-energy theorem already gives the full eΔV as the energy gained, without an extra factor of 1/2.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This introduces an unnecessary factor of two. The magnitude of the electric potential-energy change is |q|ΔV = eΔV, and by conservation of energy that equals the kinetic energy gained.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This is the signed potential-energy change, not the kinetic-energy gain. The electron (q = −e) moves to higher potential, so ΔU = qΔV = −eΔV; conservation of energy gives ΔK = −ΔU = +eΔV, and kinetic energy gained from rest cannot be negative.

stem: The voltage across a fixed resistor is doubled. Its power dissipation becomes

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This applies an inverse voltage dependence not present in resistor power.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This uses P proportional to V and misses the square.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: For fixed R, P=V²/R, so doubling voltage multiplies power by four.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This ignores the increased current and voltage across the resistor.

stem: Traversing an ideal battery from its negative terminal to its positive terminal in a loop equation contributes

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: Moving from negative to positive terminal is a potential rise of +emf.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This assigns the sign for traversing from positive to negative terminal.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: This ignores the battery's nonzero potential change.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: The battery term's sign is determined by the direction in which the loop is traversed, not by current direction.

stem: Currents 2.0 A and 3.5 A enter a junction. If one current leaves, its magnitude is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This subtracts entering currents rather than summing them.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: This averages the entering currents, which does not conserve charge flow.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Charge conservation requires outgoing current 2.0+3.5=5.5 A.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This uses only the larger incoming current and ignores the additional 2.0 A entering the junction.

stem: A capacitor in series with a resistor has been connected to a DC battery for a very long time. The circuit current is

choices.label: A
choices.rationale: This describes the instant just after connecting an initially uncharged capacitor.

choices.label: B
choices.rationale: At long time the capacitor is fully charged and behaves as an open circuit, so current is zero.

choices.label: C
choices.rationale: Infinite current is impossible here: the series resistor limits the current to at most V/R even if the capacitor were treated as a short, and at long times the fully charged capacitor blocks DC current rather than shorting it.

choices.label: D
choices.rationale: This ignores that capacitance affects the transient time, not the final DC current.
